source.title: Resurrecting the sigmoid in deep learning through dynamical isometry: theory and practice
source.authors: Jeffrey Pennington; S. Schoenholz; S. Ganguli

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental material are present; text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether initialization and nonlinearity affect training behavior, using Jacobian spectra and learning speed rather than training classification error.
record.gate_note: Reports analytical Jacobian-spectrum results and empirical learning-speed/generalization results. It does not report training classification error or test whether the networks reach near-zero training error. Cited results from other work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an original source for V4. Its own experiments directly measure learning speed under different initializations in deep plain tanh networks, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights at matched variance. Training classification error is not required to test V4's learning-speed claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, appropriately initialized orthogonal tanh networks learn orders of magnitude faster than ReLU networks in the tested CIFAR-10 setting, robustly across four optimizers. Learning time scales approximately as the square root of depth, and small nonzero q* best preserves isometry during training and gives the fastest learning and best generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Studies initialization, Jacobian conditioning, and learning speed rather than whether gradient training reaches zero or near-zero classification error. The paper also derives analytical results for Jacobian spectra.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning speed changes with initialization, nonlinearity, depth, q*, and optimizer; the authors report the relative ordering persists across optimizers. During training, the q* that best preserves isometry is a small nonzero value rather than zero.

fits_no_version.finding: Orthogonal hard-tanh networks can have well-conditioned initial Jacobians when q* is sufficiently small; orthogonal ReLU networks cannot achieve dynamical isometry in the analyzed large-width setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation and initialization jointly determine whether the full initial Jacobian spectrum concentrates near one.

fits_no_version.finding: Small nonzero initial q* best preserves isometry during training and yields the best reported generalization accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persistence of dynamical isometry during training is associated with final generalization performance.

record.peer_reviewed: 31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS 2017)
record.problems: The experiments measure test/generalization accuracy and steps to an accuracy threshold rather than training classification error. Several reported findings are qualitative descriptions of figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. Results are for a version of CIFAR-10 and do not report CIFAR-100.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted. Cited claims about deep linear networks and other prior studies are not the study's own results and were not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in convolutional networks, CIFAR-100, label corruption, and model-size or regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and student overparameterization.
Depth-related training-error degradation, identity-shortcut comparisons, the convolutional tanh initialization result, and normalization-free residual training.
The 10,000-layer convolutional result and maximum trainable depth. Experiments reach depth 300 but do not establish a trainability boundary or convergence at that depth.
Recovery above the initial stability limit, catapult loss dynamics, edge-of-stability sharpness, and divergence thresholds.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are assigned because this study is an original source for V4. Its speed results belong to V4 despite being measured through test-accuracy trajectories. The negligible orthogonal advantage at larger tanh variance is a measured condition, not grounds to reject the study's relevance.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, model size, and early stopping.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and the effect of student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual shortcut networks, depth-related training error, special initialization of plain tanh networks, and residual networks without normalization.

The study analyzes initialization effects on Jacobian conditioning and learning speed in deep networks, but does not measure training classification error or trainable depth as framed in this version.
Learning rates above the stability limit, loss rise and recovery, and sharpness during training.
Batch normalization versus no normalization, training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup.

rows.subject: ReLU networks with orthogonal weights
rows.operation_detail: Analytical maximum Jacobian singular value and eigenvalue-distribution variance at criticality
rows.measure: maximum squared singular value and variance of the eigenvalue distribution of JJT
rows.value: Both grow linearly with depth; dynamical isometry is unachievable.
rows.note: Jacobian conditioning is not training classification error, so this result does not map to V4's stated training outcomes.
rows.check: The analytical Jacobian spectrum does not itself measure learning speed or successful training depth. Retain as mechanistic evidence rather than a direct behavioral result.

rows.subject: hard-tanh networks with orthogonal weights
rows.operation_detail: Analytical maximum Jacobian singular value and eigenvalue-distribution variance at criticality
rows.measure: maximum squared singular value and variance of the eigenvalue distribution of JJT
rows.value: Dynamical isometry can be achieved up to depth L by choosing q* small enough.
rows.note: The result concerns Jacobian conditioning, not training error or the training speed/depth outcomes in V4.
rows.check: Achievable Jacobian isometry is a theoretical conditioning result, not a measurement of learning speed or successful training depth.

rows.subject: tanh networks with orthogonal weights
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning dynamics under SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, and ADAM
rows.measure: generalization performance on a test set and learning speed
rows.baseline: tanh with σw² = 2 and ReLU with σw² = 2; corresponding Gaussian initializations
rows.value: The most isometric orthogonal tanh case learns several orders of magnitude faster than the least isometric ReLU case; the ordering persists across optimizers.
rows.note: The reported measure is learning speed/generalization, not training classification error. CIFAR-10 augmentations are described in the footnote.
rows.check: Learning speed directly tests V4. Correct steps to 10^5 and batch size to 10^3. The networks are fully connected, and learning dynamics are measured through test accuracy.

rows.subject: tanh networks with Gaussian weights
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning dynamics under SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, and ADAM
rows.measure: generalization performance on a test set and learning speed
rows.value: The orthogonal and Gaussian learning curves are well-separated for the small-σw² tanh case; orthogonal initialization learns faster.
rows.note: The paper says initialization has a larger impact on learning speed than optimizer choice in this case.
rows.check: At matched weight variance, orthogonal tanh initialization learns faster than Gaussian initialization. Correct steps to 10^5 and batch size to 10^3.

rows.subject: ReLU networks with orthogonal weights
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning dynamics under SGD, Momentum, RMSProp, and ADAM
rows.measure: generalization performance on a test set and learning speed
rows.baseline: corresponding Gaussian ReLU networks and the other network classes in Figure 4
rows.value: The performance advantage of orthogonal over Gaussian initialization is expected to be somewhat negligible in this case; the least isometric ReLU networks learn several orders of magnitude slower than the most isometric orthogonal tanh case.
rows.note: Training speed and test generalization are not the training classification error claim.
rows.check: The ReLU comparison measures the several-orders-of-magnitude speed advantage of appropriately initialized orthogonal tanh networks. The negligible orthogonal-over-Gaussian advantage within ReLU is a separate comparison and should be split out if retained. Correct steps to 10^5 and batch size to 10^3.

rows.subject: orthogonal tanh networks
rows.operation_detail: Measured SGD steps to reach an accuracy threshold while varying depth
rows.value: Optimal training time is O(√L); optimal learning rate is O(1/L).
rows.note: The threshold is reported as accuracy, not training classification error.
rows.check: Steps to an accuracy threshold directly measure learning speed. The reported square-root depth scaling concerns reaching approximately 25% accuracy, not convergence or near-zero training error.

rows.subject: orthogonal tanh networks
rows.operation_detail: Measured SGD steps to reach an accuracy threshold while varying q*
rows.value: Smaller q*, associated with increased dynamical isometry, enables faster training by allowing a larger optimal learning rate.
rows.note: No training classification-error values are reported.
rows.check: Varying initialization parameters changes measured learning speed and the optimal learning rate; this directly bears on V4.

rows.subject: orthogonal tanh networks
rows.operation_detail: Tracked Jacobian singular values and their evolution during SGD training

conditions.value: 1/64; other initial q* values also considered

rows.measure: eigenvalue ill-conditioning of JJT over SGD steps, test accuracy, and generalization accuracy
rows.value: Perfect dynamical isometry at initialization (q* = 0) is not best for preserving isometry; a small but nonzero q* appears optimal, and both learning speed and generalization accuracy peak at this nonzero value.
rows.note: Figure 6 includes plots; the text gives qualitative descriptions but no numerical values for the peaks.
rows.check: The learning-speed component directly bears on V4. Separate it from spectral conditioning and final generalization accuracy. The best speed occurs at small nonzero q*, rather than perfect initial isometry.
